title: Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin
subtitle: Without the carbon bill: decarbonizing coal-heavy power and trade-exposed industry
message: A carbon tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit. A revenue-neutral feebate charges only emissions above the sector benchmark and rebates those below. Same incentive to switch; average costs almost unchanged.

problem.title: The carbon bill, not the incentive, kills the tax

stats.label: average generation cost from a $50/t tax in a stylized grid that is 60% coal

problem.text: A carbon tax sends two signals. The relative-price signal makes coal dearer than gas and solar and does the abating. The average-cost signal charges every producer for every tonne it still emits and does the political damage, so governments exempt the biggest emitters or hold the rate down.

mechanism.title: Same switch, a fraction of the cost
mechanism.caption: Change in generation cost per MWh at $50/tCO₂, stylized grid (60% coal, 20% gas, 20% solar).
points: Each producer pays t(eᵢ − ē) per unit of output: a fee above the benchmark, a rebate below.
Every tonne avoided is worth t, as under a tax, so dispatch and switching are the same.
With the benchmark at the sector average, fees fund rebates exactly: zero treasury cost.
The benchmark falls as the sector cleans, so the feebate tightens on laggards by itself.

action.title: Use feebates where carbon taxes stall
results: The treasury pays nothing; coal incumbents pay their clean competitors.
Power stays cheap under a single buyer; in a marginal-cost market, prices can rise if coal sets them.
Feebates buy fewer tonnes: about 50–70% of a tax's cuts. A consumption charge restores the demand margin.
Evidence: Swedish NOx charge cut emission rates 40% in six years; a fixed French car benchmark cost €285m.
todo: Coal-heavy countries: legislate a feebate per MWh, benchmarked to the grid average and updated yearly.
